--- title: "Exploratory data analysis" subtitle: "Session 9 · Topic 2.7 · Thu 14 Jan" format: revealjs --- ## Today ::: {.agenda} 1. What EDA is for — before any model 2. A checklist for a calculation dataset 3. One variable at a time: distributions 4. Design-space coverage 5. Relationships: scatter plots and correlation 6. Checking physics in the data 7. Writing down the findings ::: ## Setup for today ::: {#974f22ef .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd import numpy as np df = pd.read_csv("data/bracket.csv") ``` ::: ## Why EDA? > Look at the data before you fit anything. - find problems that cleaning missed - learn which inputs matter and how (linear? threshold? interaction?) - see where the design space is covered — and where it is empty - set expectations: what accuracy is realistic, which model family fits ::: {.tip} EDA is also the start of the model passport: domain of applicability, data volume, sources. ::: ## EDA checklist 1. **Structure** — rows, columns, types, IDs (Session 6) 2. **Quality** — gaps, duplicates, impossible values (Session 7) 3. **Distributions** — every input and output on its own 4. **Coverage** — how the inputs fill the design space 5. **Relationships** — inputs vs outputs, inputs vs inputs 6. **Physics** — do known trends appear in the data? 7. **Findings** — short written list with numbers # Distributions {.divider} ## Numbers first ::: {#72f1ba77 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.describe().T[["mean", "std", "min", "50%", "max"]].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
mean std min 50% max
thickness_mm 13.84 3.48 8.10 13.75 19.90
fillet_radius_mm 4.54 1.99 1.00 4.60 8.00
load_N 1592.14 835.32 203.00 1605.50 2996.00
E_GPa 200.22 5.84 190.00 199.80 210.00
max_stress_MPa 357.26 277.58 23.60 284.75 1443.10
deflection_mm 1.53 1.58 0.06 0.91 8.82
safety_factor 2.13 2.41 0.25 1.25 15.04
``` ::: ::: - mean far from median (50 %) → skewed distribution - compare min / max with the planned ranges ## Histograms {.smaller} ::: {#fb103252 .cell fig-height='4.5' fig-width='12' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.drop(columns="run_id").hist(bins=25, figsize=(12, 4.5), layout=(2, 4), color="#B0215E") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](session09-eda_files/figure-revealjs/cell-5-output-1.png){width=1299 height=477} ::: ::: - inputs: flat (uniform sampling, as planned) - outputs: **right-skewed** — many moderate values, a long tail of high stress ## Skewed outputs: try a log scale ::: {#274a6d2c .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='11' execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6)) df["deflection_mm"].hist(bins=30, ax=ax[0]); ax[0].set_title("deflection, mm") np.log10(df["deflection_mm"]).hist(bins=30, ax=ax[1]); ax[1].set_title("log10(deflection)") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](session09-eda_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=1190 height=378} ::: ::: ::: {.muted} A log transform often makes a skewed engineering output easier to model (Module 3). ::: # Design-space coverage {.divider} ## Inputs against each other ::: {#d4945807 .cell fig-height='5.2' fig-width='9' execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from pandas.plotting import scatter_matrix inputs = ["thickness_mm", "fillet_radius_mm", "load_N", "E_GPa"] scatter_matrix(df[inputs], figsize=(10, 5.2), alpha=0.5, color="#B0215E", hist_kwds={"color": "#E46A9A"}) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](session09-eda_files/figure-revealjs/cell-7-output-1.png){width=946 height=538} ::: ::: ## What to look for - empty regions → no data there → the model will **extrapolate** there - inputs correlated with each other → hard to separate their effects - clusters → the plan was not uniform ::: {#82b7e375 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} df[inputs].corr().round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
thickness_mm fillet_radius_mm load_N E_GPa
thickness_mm 1.00 0.05 -0.01 -0.07
fillet_radius_mm 0.05 1.00 -0.17 -0.00
load_N -0.01 -0.17 1.00 -0.03
E_GPa -0.07 -0.00 -0.03 1.00
``` ::: ::: ::: {.muted} Near-zero correlations between inputs: the random plan did its job. ::: # Relationships {.divider} ## Output vs each input {.smaller} ::: {#2966d26c .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='12' execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(12, 3.4), sharey=True) for a, c in zip(ax, inputs): a.scatter(df[c], df["max_stress_MPa"], s=8, alpha=.6) a.set_xlabel(c) ax[0].set_ylabel("max stress, MPa"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](session09-eda_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){width=1300 height=356} ::: ::: - strong trends with thickness and load; weaker with fillet radius; none with *E* - large scatter in each plot — the other inputs also vary ## Correlation with the outputs ::: {#68aa6063 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} cols = inputs + ["max_stress_MPa", "deflection_mm"] pd.DataFrame({ "pearson": df[cols].corr()["max_stress_MPa"], "spearman": df[cols].corr(method="spearman")["max_stress_MPa"], }).drop("max_stress_MPa").round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
pearson spearman
thickness_mm -0.62 -0.59
fillet_radius_mm -0.30 -0.27
load_N 0.67 0.77
E_GPa -0.03 0.01
deflection_mm 0.95 0.96
``` ::: ::: - **Pearson** — linear relationship; **Spearman** — any monotonic relationship - correlation ≠ importance, and ≠ cause; it only sees one input at a time ## Correlation heatmap ::: {#be034335 .cell fig-height='5' fig-width='7' execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} c = df[cols].corr() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5)) im = ax.imshow(c, cmap="RdPu", vmin=-1, vmax=1) ax.set_xticks(range(len(cols)), cols, rotation=45, ha="right"); ax.set_yticks(range(len(cols)), cols) for i in range(len(cols)): for j in range(len(cols)): ax.text(j, i, f"{c.iloc[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9) fig.colorbar(im); ax.grid(False); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](session09-eda_files/figure-revealjs/cell-11-output-1.png){width=661 height=532} ::: ::: ## Two inputs at once: colour as third dimension {.smaller} ::: {#39876228 .cell fig-height='4.5' execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5)) sc = ax.scatter(df["thickness_mm"], df["load_N"], c=df["safety_factor"].clip(upper=3), cmap="RdPu_r", s=25) fig.colorbar(sc, label="safety factor (capped at 3)") ax.set_xlabel("thickness, mm"); ax.set_ylabel("load, N"); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](session09-eda_files/figure-revealjs/cell-12-output-1.png){width=772 height=473} ::: ::: The pass / fail boundary is a curve in the (*t*, *F*) plane — not a straight line. # Checking physics {.divider} ## Does the data follow beam theory? {.smaller} Beam theory: $\delta \propto \dfrac{F}{E\,t^3}$. Combine the inputs into one variable: ::: {#7603b48a .cell fig-height='3.8' execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} df["F_over_Et3"] = df["load_N"] / (df["E_GPa"] * df["thickness_mm"] ** 3) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.8)) ax.scatter(df["F_over_Et3"], df["deflection_mm"], s=10) ax.set_xlabel("F / (E t³)"); ax.set_ylabel("deflection, mm"); plt.show() print("correlation:", round(df["F_over_Et3"].corr(df["deflection_mm"]), 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](session09-eda_files/figure-revealjs/cell-13-output-1.png){width=754 height=405} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` correlation: 1.0 ``` ::: ::: ## Why this matters - a physically motivated combined variable turns scatter into a straight line - this is **feature engineering** — often more valuable than a more complex model - if the data does **not** follow known physics → suspect the data (units, mesh, status) ::: {.tip} Your engineering knowledge is the most valuable part of an ML project. EDA is where it enters. ::: ## Writing down findings ::: {#c4d78bc2 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} n = len(df) findings = [ f"{n} converged runs; inputs uniformly cover t 8–20 mm, r 1–8 mm, F 200–3000 N, E 190–210 GPa", f"{(df.safety_factor < 1).mean():.0%} of runs exceed yield; SF ranges {df.safety_factor.min():.2f}–{df.safety_factor.max():.1f}", "stress driven by load (+) and thickness (−); fillet radius smaller effect; E no effect", "deflection is linear in F/(E t³) (r = %.3f)" % df.F_over_Et3.corr(df.deflection_mm), "outputs right-skewed → consider log transform for modelling", ] for f in findings: print("•", f) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` • 300 converged runs; inputs uniformly cover t 8–20 mm, r 1–8 mm, F 200–3000 N, E 190–210 GPa • 39% of runs exceed yield; SF ranges 0.25–15.0 • stress driven by load (+) and thickness (−); fillet radius smaller effect; E no effect • deflection is linear in F/(E t³) (r = 1.000) • outputs right-skewed → consider log transform for modelling ``` ::: ::: ## Your turn (30 min) ::: {.exercise} Full EDA of `bracket.csv` — produce a notebook with a findings list at the end. 1. Distributions of all columns; which are skewed? 2. Coverage: is there any region of (thickness, fillet radius) with few runs? 3. Relationships: which input has the strongest effect on stress? On deflection? 4. Physics: find a combination of inputs that makes **stress** linear. (Hint: nominal stress $6FL/(b t^2)$, and the fillet effect.) 5. Write 5 findings with numbers. Commit the notebook. ::: ## Summary - EDA comes **before** modelling; it finds problems and sets expectations - distributions → coverage → relationships → physics → findings - Pearson for linear, Spearman for monotonic; correlation sees one input at a time - combined physical variables (feature engineering) can make a problem almost trivial - write findings down with numbers — they become the model passport **Next session:** visualisation — making plots that are clear and honest. ## Practice at home (~1 h) - finish the EDA notebook and commit it - repeat steps 1–3 on a dataset from your own work, if you have one
